a: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?
p: The critical editions ask about being free first; the later Byzantine text asks about being an apostle first (KJV).

readings.orig: Οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐλεύθερος; οὐκ εἰμὶ ἀπόστολος;
readings.en: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?
readings.plain: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?

readings.orig: Οὐκ εἰμὶ ἀπόστολος; οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐλεύθερος;
readings.en: Am I not an apostle? Am I not free?
readings.plain: Am I not an apostle? Am I not free?

why: The Plain English Translation follows the order of the SBLGNT and NA28. The order in the Byzantine text puts the apostle question first, as it is in the next verse and in the rest of the chapter, which looks like a smoothing. The difference does not change the argument.

a: Jesus our Lord
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "Christ" after Jesus.

readings.orig: Ἰησοῦν τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν
readings.en: Jesus our Lord
readings.plain: Jesus our Lord

readings.orig: Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν
readings.en: Jesus Christ our Lord
readings.plain: Jesus Christ our Lord

why: The shorter text is in the critical editions. Scribes often lengthened names into the full title "Jesus Christ."

a: thresh in hope of a share
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "his hope" and move "in hope."

readings.orig: ὁ ἀλοῶν ἐπ᾽ ἐλπίδι τοῦ μετέχειν
readings.en: the one who threshes in hope of sharing
readings.plain: thresh in hope of a share

readings.orig: ὁ ἀλοῶν τῆς ἐλπίδος αὐτοῦ μετέχειν ἐπ᾽ ἐλπίδι
readings.en: the one who threshes to share in his hope, in hope
readings.plain: thresh in hope, to share in his hope

why: The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT and NA28. Their short phrase ("in hope of sharing") is the harder, more compressed Greek, and the Byzantine text spells out "his hope," which looks like a smoothing. The sense is close either way: the thresher shares in the crop he hopes for.

a: I would rather die than have anyone make my boast empty.
t: A broken sentence, or a repaired one?
p: The critical text breaks off in mid-sentence. Later copies smooth it.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles: the sentence breaks off (anacoluthon). The NET Bible's note lists P46, Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Claromontanus (D, first hand and a later corrector), 33, 1739 and 1881
readings.orig: καλὸν γάρ μοι μᾶλλον ἀποθανεῖν ἢ τὸ καύχημά μου οὐδεὶς κενώσει
readings.en: it is better for me to die than-- my boast no one will make empty
readings.plain: I would rather die than have anyone make my boast empty.

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV). The NET Bible's note lists Sinaiticus (a later corrector), C, Claromontanus (a later corrector), Psi, the Byzantine majority and the Latin
readings.orig: ἢ τὸ καύχημά μου ἵνα τις κενώσῃ
readings.en: than that anyone should make my boast empty
readings.plain: I would rather die than that anyone should make my boast empty.

why: The harder reading is the broken sentence, which is the one a scribe would be tempted to fix. The Plain English Translation smooths it for English, as every translation must, and the note says so.

a: my right in the good news
p: The Byzantine text adds "of Christ."

readings.orig: τῇ ἐξουσίᾳ μου ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
readings.en: my right in the good news
readings.plain: my right in the good news

readings.orig: ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ τοῦ Χριστοῦ
readings.en: in the good news of Christ
readings.plain: my right in the good news of Christ

why: The shorter text is the one the critical editions print; "of Christ" could be a scribal addition, and 9:12 has the same phrase in the genuine text.

a: like one under the law, though I am not myself under the law
t: "Though I am not myself under the law"
p: Paul's clause about himself is missing from the Byzantine text and the KJV.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles. The NET Bible's note lists Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, C, Claromontanus (first hand), F, G, P, 33, 104, 365, 1175, 1505, 1739 and the Latin
readings.orig: ὡς ὑπὸ νόμον, μὴ ὢν αὐτὸς ὑπὸ νόμον
readings.en: as under the law, though not myself under the law
readings.plain: like one under the law, though I am not myself under the law

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV). The NET Bible's note lists Claromontanus (a later corrector), Psi, 1881 and the Byzantine majority
readings.orig: ὡς ὑπὸ νόμον
readings.en: as under the law
readings.plain: like one under the law

why: The longer reading is in the critical editions and is hard to explain as an addition. The eye of a copyist could easily skip from one "under the law" to the next, which would produce the shorter text. The clause matters because it shows that Paul does not count himself bound by the law as a Jew would be.

a: though I am not outside God's law but under Christ's law
p: The Byzantine text says Paul is not "without law toward God" but "under law toward Christ."

readings.orig: μὴ ὢν ἄνομος θεοῦ ἀλλ᾽ ἔννομος Χριστοῦ
readings.en: not being without God's law but within Christ's law
readings.plain: though I am not outside God's law but under Christ's law

readings.orig: μὴ ὢν ἄνομος θεῷ ἀλλ᾽ ἔννομος Χριστῷ
readings.en: not being without law toward God but under law toward Christ
readings.plain: though I am not outside the law toward God but under the law toward Christ

why: The genitives are in the critical editions' text. The datives are the more natural Greek for "toward God," which suggests a smoothing. The change is small, but the genitive makes "Christ's law" a thing and not just a direction.

a: To the weak I became weak
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say Paul became "as weak," not simply weak.

readings.orig: ἐγενόμην τοῖς ἀσθενέσιν ἀσθενής
readings.en: I became to the weak, weak
readings.plain: To the weak I became weak

readings.orig: ἐγενόμην τοῖς ἀσθενέσιν ὡς ἀσθενής
readings.en: I became to the weak as weak
readings.plain: To the weak I became as weak

why: The Plain English Translation follows the critical editions. The Byzantine "as" (hos) brings the line into the pattern of 9:20-21, "like a Jew," "like one under the law," and so looks like a harmonizing addition. It changes the sense: with "as," Paul acts like the weak without being weak; without it, he says he became weak himself.

a: I do everything for the sake of the good news
p: The critical text says "all things"; the Byzantine text, behind the KJV, says "this."

readings.orig: πάντα δὲ ποιῶ διὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον
readings.en: all things I do for the sake of the good news
readings.plain: I do everything for the sake of the good news

readings.orig: τοῦτο δὲ ποιῶ διὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον
readings.en: this I do for the sake of the good news
readings.plain: I do this for the sake of the good news

why: "All things" fits the whole section on becoming all things to all (9:19-22), and the Byzantine "this" would be a natural narrowing by copyists.

a: Brothers, I want you to know this
p: The critical editions open 10:1 with "for"; the Byzantine text and the KJV open with "moreover."

readings.orig: Οὐ θέλω γὰρ ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοί
readings.en: for I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers
readings.plain: Brothers, I want you to know this

readings.orig: Οὐ θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοί
readings.en: now I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers
readings.plain: Now, brothers, I want you to know this

why: The Plain English Translation follows the critical editions, in which "for" gives the wilderness story as the reason for the warning of 9:24-27. "Now" starts a new topic, which looks like a smoothing. The Plain English Translation leaves the connective out of the English and starts a new sentence.

a: baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea
p: NA28 has a passive verb; the SBLGNT and the other editions have a middle. The English is the same.

readings.w: SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Textus Receptus and Byzantine text (middle). The NET Bible's note lists a later corrector of P46, Vaticanus, 1739, 1881, the Byzantine majority and Origen, and says the first hand of P46 has the imperfect middle ebaptizonto
readings.orig: εἰς τὸν Μωϋσῆν ἐβαπτίσαντο
readings.en: they had themselves baptized into Moses
readings.plain: baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea

readings.w: NA28 (as in NA27): passive. The NET Bible's note lists Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, C, Claromontanus, F, G, Psi, 33 and the Latin
readings.orig: εἰς τὸν Μωϋσῆν ἐβαπτίσθησαν
readings.en: they were baptized into Moses
readings.plain: baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea

why: The Plain English Translation follows the SBLGNT, but both verbs read the same in English: Israel was baptized into Moses. The passive is the usual form for baptism elsewhere in Paul (Romans 6:3; 1 Corinthians 12:13), so it may be a change toward the familiar wording, though NA28 prints it.

a: put the Christ to the test
p: Manuscripts divide over whom Israel tested in the wilderness: Christ, the Lord, or God.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV). The NET Bible's note lists P46, Claromontanus, F, G, 1739, 1881, Psi, the Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions and says the reading is in the majority of manuscripts
readings.orig: ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν Χριστόν
readings.en: let us not test the Christ
readings.plain: put the Christ to the test

readings.w: THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles. The NET Bible's note lists Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, C, P, 33, 104 and 1175
readings.orig: ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν κύριον
readings.en: let us not test the Lord
readings.plain: put the Lord to the test

readings.w: The NET Bible's note lists Alexandrinus (A) and 81
readings.orig: ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν θεόν
readings.en: let us not test God
readings.plain: put God to the test

why: The Plain English Translation follows "the Christ," the reading of the SBLGNT and NA28 as well as the Byzantine text. The Christ reading is the hardest, since it puts Christ in the wilderness, and it matches 10:4 ("that rock was the Christ"). "Lord" or "God" is what a scribe would be tempted to write, since Numbers 21 says Israel spoke against God. The case for "Lord" is not weak: the NET Bible's note itself says that some of the important Alexandrian witnesses have "Lord," and the editors of THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles chose it. The witness lists above are those printed in the NET Bible's note. The Numbers story: "the LORD sent the burning snakes among the people" (Numbers 21:6). Compare Jude 5, where manuscripts also divide over Jesus, the Lord and God.

a: These things kept happening to them as examples
p: The critical editions have the adverb "typologically"; the Byzantine text and the KJV have "all" and the noun "examples."

readings.orig: ταῦτα δὲ τυπικῶς συνέβαινεν ἐκείνοις
readings.en: now these things were happening to them as a pattern
readings.plain: These things kept happening to them as examples

readings.orig: ταῦτα δὲ πάντα τύποι συνέβαινον ἐκείνοις
readings.en: now all these things were happening to them as examples
readings.plain: All these things happened to them as examples

why: The Plain English Translation follows the critical editions. The adverb typikos is found only here in the New Testament, and the Byzantine noun typoi repeats 10:6, which looks like a smoothing toward the earlier verse. The Plain English Translation's sense is the same either way.

a: what they sacrifice
p: The Gentiles are named in some manuscripts and in the KJV. The SBLGNT and NA28 leave them out.

readings.orig: ἃ θύουσιν, δαιμονίοις καὶ οὐ θεῷ θύουσιν
readings.en: what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God
readings.plain: what they sacrifice

readings.w: THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἃ θύουσιν τὰ ἔθνη, δαιμονίοις καὶ οὐ θεῷ θύουσιν
readings.en: what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God
readings.plain: what the Gentiles sacrifice

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter SBLGNT, which is the text of the SBL and NA28. The longer text adds the subject the sentence already implies from verse 18, and the editors who prefer it (THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles) take the omission to be an accident. The meaning is the same.

a: "Everything is lawful," but not everything is helpful. "Everything is lawful," but not everything builds up.
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "for me" both times, as at 6:12.

readings.orig: Πάντα ἔξεστιν ἀλλ᾽ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει· πάντα ἔξεστιν ἀλλ᾽ οὐ πάντα οἰκοδομεῖ
readings.en: all things are lawful, but not all things are helpful; all things are lawful, but not all things build up
readings.plain: "Everything is lawful," but not everything is helpful. "Everything is lawful," but not everything builds up.

readings.orig: Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν ἀλλ᾽ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει· πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν ἀλλ᾽ οὐ πάντα οἰκοδομεῖ
readings.en: all things are lawful for me, but not all things are helpful; all things are lawful for me, but not all things build up
readings.plain: "Everything is lawful for me," but not everything is helpful. "Everything is lawful for me," but not everything builds up.

why: The shorter text is the one the critical editions print. "For me" is in the genuine text of 6:12, and copyists would easily bring 10:23 into line with it.

a: No one should look for his own good, but for the good of the other person.
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "each" at the end.

readings.orig: μηδεὶς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ζητείτω ἀλλὰ τὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου
readings.en: let no one seek his own, but that of the other
readings.plain: No one should look for his own good, but for the good of the other person.

readings.orig: μηδεὶς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ζητείτω, ἀλλὰ τὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου ἕκαστος
readings.en: let no one seek his own, but each that of the other
readings.plain: No one should look for his own good, but each one for the good of the other.

why: The shorter text is the one the critical editions print. "Each" (hekastos) completes the second clause and is the kind of smoothing a scribe adds.

a: because of conscience.
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add a second quotation of Psalm 24:1 at the end of 10:28.

readings.orig: καὶ τὴν συνείδησιν
readings.en: and because of conscience
readings.plain: because of conscience.

readings.orig: καὶ τὴν συνείδησιν· τοῦ γὰρ κυρίου ἡ γῆ καὶ τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῆς
readings.en: and because of conscience; for the earth is the Lord's and its fullness
readings.plain: because of conscience. For the earth and all that fills it belong to the Lord.

why: The Psalm is already quoted in 10:26 where it fits. The copyists most likely repeated it to give a reason for the host's rule.

a: This is from a sacrifice
t: "Offered to idols" in the Byzantine text
p: The Byzantine text and KJV replace "from a sacrifice" with "offered to idols."

readings.orig: ἱερόθυτόν
readings.en: sacrificed in a holy rite
readings.plain: This is from a sacrifice

readings.orig: εἰδωλόθυτόν
readings.en: offered to idols
readings.plain: This is offered to idols

why: The rarer pagan word is the one found in the critical texts. Scribes would naturally bring the sentence into line with Paul's own term in chapters 8-10.

a: I praise you that you remember me in everything
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "brothers" in 11:2.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles. The NET Bible's note lists P46, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, C, P, 81, 630, 1175, 1739, 1881, 2464 and the Coptic
readings.orig: Ἐπαινῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς ὅτι πάντα μου μέμνησθε
readings.en: I praise you that you remember me in everything
readings.plain: I praise you that you remember me in everything

readings.w: Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV). The NET Bible's note lists Claromontanus, F, G, Psi, 33, the Byzantine majority, the Latin and Syriac
readings.orig: Ἐπαινῶ δὲ ὑμᾶς, ἀδελφοί, ὅτι πάντα μου μέμνησθε
readings.en: I praise you, brothers, that you remember me in everything
readings.plain: I praise you, brothers, that you remember me in everything

why: The shorter text is the one the critical editions print, and the NET Bible's note prefers it. "Brothers" is a typical addition at the start of a new section, which is why it is easy to add and hard to explain as an omission.

a: he gave thanks, broke it, and said, "This is my body, which is for you.
p: The KJV has "Take, eat" and "which is broken for you." The SBLGNT and NA28 do not.

readings.orig: εὐχαριστήσας ἔκλασεν καὶ εἶπεν· Τοῦτό μού ἐστιν τὸ σῶμα τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν
readings.en: having given thanks he broke it and said: this is my body that is for you
readings.plain: he gave thanks, broke it, and said, "This is my body, which is for you.

readings.orig: εὐχαριστήσας ἔκλασεν καὶ εἶπεν· Λάβετε φάγετε· τοῦτό μού ἐστιν τὸ σῶμα τὸ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κλώμενον
readings.en: having given thanks he broke it and said: take, eat; this is my body that is for you, broken
readings.plain: he gave thanks, broke it, and said, "Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you.

why: The shorter text is the one the critical editions print. "Take, eat" comes from Matthew 26:26, and "broken" fits the breaking of the bread; both are what a copyist would add from the Gospel and from the action. The shorter reading is the one the Plain English Translation follows.

a: drink the cup
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say "this cup."

readings.orig: καὶ τὸ ποτήριον πίνητε
readings.en: and drink the cup
readings.plain: drink the cup

readings.orig: καὶ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο πίνητε
readings.en: and drink this cup
readings.plain: drink this cup

why: The shorter text is the one the critical editions print. "This" matches "this bread" in the same sentence and is an easy addition. The meaning is the same.

a: eats the bread
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say "this bread" in 11:27.

readings.orig: ὃς ἂν ἐσθίῃ τὸν ἄρτον
readings.en: whoever eats the bread
readings.plain: eats the bread

readings.orig: ὃς ἂν ἐσθίῃ τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον
readings.en: whoever eats this bread
readings.plain: eats this bread

why: The shorter text is the one the critical editions print; "this" is an easy addition from verse 26 ("this bread"). The meaning is the same. Note that every Greek edition on this site, the Textus Receptus included, reads "or" (e) between the bread and the cup; the KJV's "and" is its rendering. The point matters for the debate over communion in one kind or both: "or" lets a person offend by eating or drinking alone, and has been read as treating either half as enough, while "and" would join them. The churches' views are on the card at 11:27-29.

a: For the one who eats and drinks eats and drinks judgment on himself if he does not discern the body.
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "unworthily" and "the Lord's" in 11:29.

readings.orig: ὁ γὰρ ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων κρίμα ἑαυτῷ ἐσθίει καὶ πίνει μὴ διακρίνων τὸ σῶμα
readings.en: for the one who eats and drinks eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning the body
readings.plain: For the one who eats and drinks eats and drinks judgment on himself if he does not discern the body.

readings.orig: ὁ γὰρ ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων ἀναξίως κρίμα ἑαυτῷ ἐσθίει καὶ πίνει μὴ διακρίνων τὸ σῶμα τοῦ κυρίου
readings.en: for the one who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself, not discerning the Lord's body
readings.plain: For the one who eats and drinks in an unworthy way eats and drinks judgment on himself if he does not discern the Lord's body.

why: The shorter text is the one the critical editions print. Both additions could be expansions from verse 27. They do change the sense: with "the Lord's body" the eucharistic reading is easier to hear; the shorter text leaves the "body" open.

a: But if we judged ourselves, we would not come under judgment.
p: The critical editions have "but"; the Byzantine text and the KJV have "for."

readings.orig: εἰ δὲ ἑαυτοὺς διεκρίνομεν
readings.en: but if we judged ourselves
readings.plain: But if we judged ourselves, we would not come under judgment.

readings.orig: Εἰ γὰρ ἑαυτοὺς διεκρίνομεν
readings.en: for if we judged ourselves
readings.plain: For if we judged ourselves, we would not come under judgment.

why: The Plain English Translation follows the critical editions, where "but" sets self-judgment against the judgment of 11:30. "For" reads as a smoother explanation of the verse before it, which looks like a smoothing.
